title: Portland just launched the most delightfully weird scavenger hunt you'll see this year — and it involves a 200-pound ballerina Sasquatch
byline: Sean Sterling | The Oregonian/OregonLiveOpens in new window
excerpt: More than 25 local artists have hidden Bigfoot-inspired creations across 21 Portland locations.
content:
According to the Bigfoot Field Researchers Organization (BFRO), there have been 254 verified Bigfoot sightings in Oregon. Thanks to Geek Week PDX and its devotion to all things “nerdy,” those numbers are about to climb.

A citywide scavenger hunt is sending Oregonians in search of Sasquatch during the month of September, with local artists hiding Bigfoot-inspired artwork in storefronts, public spaces and cultural landmarks.

The Sneaky Squatch PDX Art Hunt launched September 8 with the unveiling of an 8-foot-tall Sasquatch sculpture at Portland City Hall.

Built by Moni and Rick Sears of Goblin Art from recycled and reclaimed cardboard, the towering figure serves as both a selfie stop and a launch point for the broader pop-up art adventure. The Sasquatch hunt is tied to Geek Week PDX, which runs Sept. 11–20.

Organizers said the hunt is designed to showcase Portland artists and small businesses while giving participants a playful reason to explore spots they may not otherwise visit. The citywide installation features work from more than 25 local artists, with pieces ranging from coin-sized creatures to a 200-pound ballerina Sasquatch.

To find the furry friends, participants are encouraged to download the Sneaky Sasquatch game book, which provides simple clues on where to start their search.

Once spotted in the wild, each Sasquatch also includes a nearby QR code with details about the artist, the piece itself and any hirsute neighbors within walking distance. Participants can start wherever they like, solve clues at their own pace and decide how deep into the quest they want to go.

The concept began after a Geek Week PDX volunteer suggested the scavenger-hunt format for a Portland art crawl. Organizers initially expected a small group of contributors.

“We only did one call to ask for artists,” said Amy Monthercraft, who describes herself as the chief art goblin of Geek Week PDX. “We really never thought the idea would become so big.”

Instead, the call drew a large response from creators eager to reinterpret the Northwest legend in their own styles. “It’s just a reflection of how amazing and creative and just wonderful people are in Portland,” said Monthercraft.

Among the works are Stevie Jablonsky’s mural “Sasquatch Blues” at Urbanite and Kassy Lopez’s 200-pound ballerina sculpture “In the Wild Mythical Dance” at the Keller Auditorium fountains.

Jablonsky heard about the gig after doing some work on Alberta’s Happy Alley Community Art Walk.

She said her Urbanite mural took two full days. “It was a little bit toasty, so I had to split it up.”

Lopez, meanwhile, was approached because of her cryptozoological credentials. She was invited to participate after creating a Loch Ness Monster sculpture in Milwaukie. “They were like, hey, we heard about this, and we want you to make something for the Sasquatch,” Lopez said.

Other displays include Amanda Stamatelaky’s three-eyed “Primordial Squatch” inside Sinister Coffee, Caitlin McNamara’s miniature creature hidden at the Heathman Hotel and Dave Castr’s comic-book twist with “Sasquatchu looking at?” at Books with Pictures.

Concerned about all these spoiler alerts? Not to worry. There are still oodles of mystery locations to find furry friends. “We want you to go out and find your new favorite artist,” Monthercraft said. “We want you to go out and find your new favorite shop. We want you to really explore.”

Geek Week PDX, now in its third year, celebrates Portland’s fan culture through events tied to comics, gaming, technology, science, cosplay and other creative communities. Founder David Raycroft hopes that the Sneaky Squatch PDX Art Hunt is something a random passerby can stumble onto, chase around with some friends and then fold the fun of it all into a larger week of events.
